title: The paper has no wage, welfare, or labor-market payoff, yet the introduction twice promises one
location: 1_introduction.tex lines 104 and 108; 3_shortrun.tex Sec 3.3; 5_longrun.tex eq (6); A_omitted_proofs.tex Lemma OA-1 (Sec A.3); B_macro_production.tex Sec B.2
claim: The introduction asserts twice that the model speaks to factor prices: "The AI chaining feature of the model implies that improvements in AI quality can generate non-monotone effects on labor demand and wages" (1_introduction.tex:104) and "reallocating steps between humans and AI and thus changing labor demand and wages" (:108). Nothing in the paper delivers this. In the short run the wage is normalized away by fiat (3_shortrun.tex: "we normalize it to 1"), so eq (1) is a pure time-minimization. In the long run the wage is not derived but assumed: "We then assume that a worker's wage is proportional to the skill level of their job," eq (6) Wage_j = sum of skill costs, with no labor supply, no market clearing, and no outside option. The non-monotonicity result (Lemma OA-1) is entirely about the firm's cost function, g*(alpha) = -dC*/dalpha, a derivative of production cost, not of labor demand or of any wage. Appendix B carries w_A and w_M as exogenous parameters throughout and never closes the labor market. Grepping the entire body plus Appendix B for "welfare", "inequality", "labor share", "unemploy", or "policy" returns zero hits.
why_it_matters: ReStud's first question of a task-model paper is what it says about factor prices, the labor share, or welfare that Acemoglu-Restrepo does not. As written the answer is nothing: the model is a firm-level cost-minimization over configurations of a fixed workflow, with wages either normalized to one or imposed by assumption. That makes this an organization-design/operations paper wearing task-model clothing, and it makes the title's second half ("Redefining Work") and the intro's labor-demand claims unsupported. Every sentence in the intro and conclusion linking chaining to wages must currently be struck, which guts the framing.
already_addressed: Partially, in the sense that the authors clearly know the gap: Section 5.1 footnote (foot:wage) concedes "Rather than formalizing such a wage model here, we impose this as an assumption" and defers to Appendix B; Section 6.1 offers the CES aggregation as the bridge to macro. But Appendix B stops at deriving the functional form in eq (11); it never solves for w_A, w_M, never computes a labor share, and never does a comparative static in alpha. So the deferral chain (body -> Sec 6.1 -> App B) terminates without the object it was deferring to.
fix: Either (a) close the model: put a labor supply side on the two labor types of Appendix B, solve for w_A/w_M, and derive at least one comparative static in AI quality alpha, ideally showing that the reorganization thresholds of Section 4.3 produce discrete jumps in the AI-management wage premium and in the relative demand for verification skill (this is the natural and genuinely novel result the chaining structure buys you: verification skill is a fixed cost per chain, so its return is non-monotone in alpha in a way no CES task model generates); or (b) drop the labor-demand-and-wage language from lines 104 and 108, from the conclusion, and from the title, and reframe the paper honestly as a theory of AI deployment within a fixed workflow. Option (a) is what makes it a ReStud paper.

title: Section 5, the half of the paper the title advertises, contains no formal result and is excluded from the empirics by the authors themselves
claim: Section 5 runs seven body pages and contains zero propositions, lemmas, corollaries, or comparative statics: grep for theorem environments across 5_longrun.tex returns nothing. It sets up skill costs, eq (6) for wages, eq (8) for the wage bill, hand-off costs h_i, and eq (10) for the long-run program, then delivers a geometric picture and one hand-picked three-task numerical example (skill/time/hand-off = (3,1,3), (1,2,0.5), (2,2,0)) whose four job designs are enumerated in Appendix D. Its one substantive claim about AI is immediately withdrawn: "The net effect of AI on job breadth is therefore an empirical question our framework poses rather than settles" (5_longrun.tex:236). Meanwhile 7_empirics.tex opens by ruling the section out of the empirical evaluation: "The predictions we take to the data are those of the short-run problem... not enough time has passed since the AI tools became widely available for such reorganization to have worked its way into the data." The only formal result touching eq (10) is Proposition 4, which is a running-time bound.
why_it_matters: Seven pages of new primitives (skill costs, hand-off costs, job designs) are introduced, proved nothing with, and tested nothing with. A referee reads this as an unfinished second paper stapled on, and it is the direct cause of the title and abstract overpromising "Redefining Work." It also creates the internal contradiction in Finding 6: Section 4 is written in skill-weighted costs that only exist because Section 5 exists.
already_addressed: The authors flag the empirical exclusion openly in 7_empirics.tex and describe it as "a deliberate restriction rather than a limitation of the theory," and Appendix D.1 supplies the example's cost table. But nowhere do they supply a theoretical result. There is no proposition on how the optimal number of jobs p* moves with alpha, no condition under which chaining widens versus narrows jobs, and no characterization of which steps become job boundaries.
fix: Deliver the one result the section is set up for and cannot currently state: a comparative static on job breadth in alpha. Something of the form: holding hand-off costs fixed, the optimal job design coarsens (weakly fewer job boundaries) as alpha rises, because a chain strips the skill of its automated steps out of the wage rate, and characterize the threshold at which a boundary is dissolved in terms of h_i versus the skill saved. If that result is not available, cut Section 5 to a two-page extension in the appendix and change the title.

title: This is a theory-CS paper and an LLM-measurement paper merged; 49 of the 77 appendix pages serve 11 pages of body, and Section 6.1/Appendix B assumes away the paper's own mechanism
location: 0_main.tex structure; 6_extensions.tex Sec 6.1 (p.31) and footnote at line 25; B_macro_production.tex (OA-19 to OA-28); Secs 6.2 + A.4-A.5; Appendices C-H (OA-29 to OA-77)
claim: The body divides into four essentially separable products: (i) the chaining model and its three implications, Secs 3-4, 14pp; (ii) the long-run job-design apparatus, Sec 5, 7pp; (iii) two dynamic-programming complexity results, Sec 6.2 + Props 3-4, whose content is O(m^2) and a (1+eps)-approximation in O(m^2 eps^-2 log^2(mB)); (iv) the O*NET/Eloundou/Anthropic/GPT empirical exercise, Sec 7, 11pp, supported by 49 pages of appendix (C through H). Section 6.1 is the clearest case for the knife: the CES representation is entirely in Appendix B, and the paper's own footnote concedes the representation "asks more of the economy than the firm-level argument does: capital productivity is common across firms, every firm organizes identically, and realized effective AI quality is the single dimension along which firms differ" (6_extensions.tex:25). "Every firm organizes identically" is precisely the negation of the paper's thesis, and the text then admits "The organizational content carries over as well, but only in the parameters" (:36). So ten appendix pages are spent showing that the paper's mechanism is invisible in the aggregate representation.
why_it_matters: A ReStud referee asks "is this one paper?" The answer here is no, and the diagnosis matters because the wrong cuts would be made otherwise. The CES aggregation contributes nothing to the thesis (it is a Houthakker-Levhari exercise that would be publishable, or not, on its own), the DP propositions are algorithms with no economic content that will read to an economics referee as evidence of a CS co-author's paper showing through, and the empirical exercise has a 5:1 appendix-to-body ratio that signals the measurement is doing more work than the theory.
already_addressed: Section 6 opens by acknowledging it collects "two additional results that the framework delivers, but defers their detailed discussion to the appendix," and 6.1 offers a justification ("micro and macro representations of production are therefore not in competition"). That justification is exactly the problem: not being in competition is not a contribution.
fix: Cut Section 6.1 and Appendix B entirely and spin them off, or at minimum reduce them to one paragraph in the conclusion noting the framework nests into a CES aggregate. Compress Section 6.2 to a single paragraph plus Propositions 3-4 stated in a remark, with the proofs staying in Appendix A. Reallocate the freed 4-5 body pages to (a) the wage/welfare result of Finding 1 and (b) promoting the strongest external-validation evidence from Appendix H into Section 7, which is currently the paper's most credible material and is buried at OA-65. Journal-fit recommendation: as currently structured this is not a ReStud paper, because the theoretical contribution is a cost-minimization over contiguous partitions with an approximation bound and a complexity result, and the empirics have no identifying variation. With Finding 1 fixed it becomes a plausible ReStud submission. Absent that fix, the natural home is AEJ: Macro or JOLE, or, if the authors instead lead with the O*NET/Anthropic measurement and the LLM-sequencing validation of Appendix H, an empirical outlet; ACM EC would take the DP and approximation material, which is presumably where it came from.

title: The three "tests" are noise-rejection checks framed as tests, Prediction #1 is a definitional consequence, and the observed chain length of 1.45 means the model's central object is essentially absent from the data
location: Abstract, 0_main.tex; 7_empirics.tex Secs 7.1 and 7.3; 4_implications.tex eq (7) versus 7_empirics.tex EFI definition
claim: Three problems compound. (a) Prediction #1 is not an implication, it is a definition: 7_empirics.tex says it "follows from our definition of AI chains (Definition~\ref{def:ai_chain}), which requires every automated step to be followed by another automated or augmented step." The model cannot generate non-contiguous AI execution, so contiguity in the data cannot discriminate the model from anything. (b) The placebos only reject pure noise, which the paper concedes: "We emphasize that these tests rule out either input being pure noise. In particular, they do not establish that the GPT task orderings we use are the 'right' ones" (7_empirics.tex:79). (c) The magnitude undercuts the mechanism. Observed mean chain length is 1.45, and by the paper's own convention "An AI-augmented step is thus an AI chain of length one" (3_shortrun.tex) with zero automated steps. So the modal AI run in the data contains no automation, no verification is saved, and the entire engine of the paper is not observed operating. Section 7.3 says so out loud: "consistent with the relatively short average AI chain length observed in the data (mean length 1.45), implying that tasks two positions away rarely fall in the same chain." Separately, Proposition 2 is never taken to the data: the theoretical fragmentation index of eq (7) is a probability-weighted expected cost over random failure sets F and components C_j, whereas the EFI of Section 7.2 is a deterministic count ratio (potential tasks / total steps) with no q_i, no manual times, and no expectation. They are different objects, so Proposition 2's bound (OPT/8 <= FI <= 5OPT/4) supports nothing that is estimated. Against this, the abstract asserts "Empirical evidence supports the model's key predictions."
why_it_matters: ReStud holds empirics to an identification bar, and there is no identifying variation here: exposure, execution, and ordering are all imputed or borrowed, and the only counterfactual is a within-occupation reshuffle. The abstract's "supports the model's key predictions" and the intro's "We test, and find evidence consistent with, three key predictions" will read as overclaiming once a referee reaches 7_empirics.tex:79. Worse, the 1.45 number means a referee can say the paper's data show augmentation, not chaining.
already_addressed: Substantially, and to the authors' credit: the noise-only caveat is stated, Appendix F re-runs everything under ten prompts, Appendix G prunes to frequently-executed tasks, Appendix H validates the sequencing externally, and footnote to Sec 7.2 concedes EFI Definition 2 "is mechanically related to the dependent variable." What is missing is (i) any acknowledgment that Prediction #1 is definitional, (ii) any reporting of the chain-length distribution rather than the mean, so the reader can see what fraction of AI runs have length >= 2 and therefore involve any automation at all, and (iii) any statement that the estimated EFI is not the FI of Proposition 2.
fix: Three concrete changes. First, downgrade the language throughout: "consistent with" and "we do not claim to identify" in the abstract, intro, and Sec 7 opening; drop "test" for Prediction #1 and call it a descriptive fact. Second, report the full distribution of AI-run lengths, the share of AI-executed steps sitting in runs of length >= 2, and the implied number of steps that are automated rather than augmented under the model's mapping; if that share is small, say so and explain what the model still buys. Third, either derive the EFI from eq (7) as a special case (e.g. state it as the FI at q_i in {0,1} and m_i >= 1, if that is what it is) or rename it so no reader believes Proposition 2 is being tested, and add the derivation to Appendix D.

title: The body reports the external validation's best number and omits its worst; Prediction #3 has no external validation at all and the main text does not say so
location: 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.4 lines 305-312; 1_introduction.tex final paragraph; H_external_validation.tex Secs H.2 and H.3 (OA-74 to OA-77)
claim: Appendix H is the paper's most valuable and most candid material, and the body systematically softens it. Sec 7.4 says "The LLM recovers a large majority of the benchmark precedences in both corpora" and the intro says "Our LLM sequencing recovers both to a substantial degree." Neither the body nor the intro reports the headline statistic, which Appendix H.3 states plainly: the orderings "agree with each other at an average pairwise tau of 0.79, well above the 0.53 they achieve against APQC, so the instrument is considerably more self-consistent than it is accurate." A mean Kendall tau of 0.53 against the only practitioner benchmark is the number a referee will want, and it appears once, on OA-77. Separately, Sec 7.4's closing sentence lists only "Predictions #1 and #2 come through" on the transferred PCF corpus, without saying why #3 is absent; Appendix H.2 explains: "We do not attempt a counterpart of the neighbor-execution regression... only 9 [DWAs] contain both an AI-executed and a non-executed step... underpowered for that exercise by roughly an order of magnitude." Prediction #3 is the paper's cleanest and most-emphasized empirical result (it is the one Proposition 1 points to, at 4_implications.tex:99) and it is the one with no external check.
why_it_matters: A referee who reads the appendix after the body concludes the body is spinning. That is a credibility loss out of proportion to the underlying facts, which are respectable. It also matters substantively: Prediction #3 is the test whose design most depends on the ordering being correct, since it is defined entirely over immediate neighbors, and it is exactly the test the validation cannot reach.
already_addressed: Appendix H is thorough and self-critical: it flags that the benchmarks "validate the ordering procedure rather than the specific O*NET orderings," that the PCF is "weighted toward enterprise process work," and that some disagreement "is indeterminacy in the benchmark rather than error." The problem is entirely one of what crosses into the body.
fix: Put the numbers in Section 7.4: the mean tau against APQC, the pairwise self-consistency tau, the share of pairs placed in the practitioners' direction, and one sentence saying the instrument is more self-consistent than accurate. Add one sentence stating that Prediction #3 could not be externally validated for lack of within-DWA execution variation in the matched corpus, and say what that leaves open. This costs half a page and converts the appendix from a liability into the paper's strongest defensive asset.

title: Equation (2), which carries the paper's headline result, is priced in an objective that is neither the short-run nor the long-run cost, and uses skill notation defined two sections later
location: 4_implications.tex eq (2) (eq:ca_test, line 18) and the decomposition at lines 40-48; versus 3_shortrun.tex eq (1) and Table 1 notes; versus 5_longrun.tex eq (8); versus A_omitted_proofs.tex Sec A.1 (V_0 through V_3)
claim: Section 4 is billed as the implications of the short-run problem, but eq (2) compares "c^A_{k+1} a_{k+1} / (q_k q_{k+1})" against "c^M_k m_k + c^A_{k+1} a_{k+1} / q_{k+1}", i.e. it prices every step at a skill-times-time product. Three inconsistencies follow. (i) Section 3 states the opposite: the notes to Table 1 say "This is all the short-run problem requires: with the whole workflow assigned to one worker at a fixed wage, execution time is the only margin and no notion of skill is needed," and eq (1) is min over T of the sum of t_b alone. (ii) The skill symbols c^M_i and c^A_i are used nine times in 4_implications.tex and are first defined in 5_longrun.tex, seven pages later. (iii) The appendix proof of the very proposition eq (2) motivates prices the same four arrangements in pure time: V_0 = mu_{k-1} + m_k + mu_{k+1}, V_1 = mu_{k-1} + a_{k+1}/(q_k q_{k+1}), etc., with no skill terms anywhere, and Proposition 1's hypothesis is the pure-time condition m_k < a_k/q_k. Note also that the skill-weighted objective in eq (2) is not the long-run objective either: eq (8) is (sum of skills) times (sum of times) for a job, not a sum of per-task products, so eq (2) corresponds to no optimization problem stated in the paper.
why_it_matters: Equation (2) is the single most important equation in the paper, the one the abstract's headline claim rests on. A referee who checks it against eq (1) and against the Appendix A proof finds three different objective functions and will not trust the rest. It also reads as evidence of Finding 2's underlying problem: Section 4 was written against a long-run objective and the paper was later restructured around the short run without reconciling the notation.
already_addressed: Nothing found. Grepping every .tex for a reconciliation of the skill-weighted per-task cost with either eq (1) or eq (8) returns nothing; Table 1's notes and Table 2's notes assert the split cleanly but eq (2) violates it. Footnote 8 in 4_implications.tex extends eq (2) to composite chains using "management cost c^A_r a_r", propagating the same inconsistency.
fix: Set c^M and c^A to 1 throughout Section 4 so eq (2) reads a_{k+1}(1-q_k)/(q_k q_{k+1}) < m_k, matching eq (1), Example 1's parameters (m_i, a_i, q_i), Figure 5, and the Appendix A proof. If the skill-weighted version is wanted, state it as a remark after Section 5.1 with the correct long-run objective from eq (8), and note explicitly there that Proposition 1 is proved for the time-only case. Then sweep 4_implications.tex for the nine skill occurrences and footnote 8.

title: No roadmap, no first-page "we show" paragraph, a three-page standalone literature section before the model, and a conclusion that only restates
claim: Grepping all .tex files for "proceeds as follows", "organized as follows", "remainder of the paper", or "rest of the paper" returns nothing: a 45-page body with a 77-page appendix has no roadmap. The introduction's first page is entirely setup (task-model literature, the steps/tasks/jobs vocabulary); the headline result does not get its own paragraph until the "Optimizing Automation and Fragmentation" heading on p.5, and there is no compact "we show X, Y, Z" statement anywhere. Related Literature is a standalone Section 2 running pp.7-10, so the reader waits until p.10 for the model. The abstract's final clause sells the CES aggregation, an appendix result the paper itself says preserves the organizational content "only in the parameters" (6_extensions.tex:36), which means the abstract's last promise is the paper's weakest contribution. The conclusion is fifteen lines that restate Sections 4.1, 5, 4.3, and 7 in order, with no limitations, no open questions, and no research agenda; the one forward-looking sentence in the paper sits in Section 6.2 instead ("the algorithms above could be run on real workflows to ask how a given advance in AI capability would redraw them"). Keywords and JEL codes are commented out in 0_main.tex.
why_it_matters: These compound with Finding 3: a reader who cannot see the architecture in the first two pages and gets no roadmap will experience the 45 body pages as sprawl rather than as a plan, which is precisely the impression that sinks papers described as "two papers merged." The abstract ending on the weakest result is a first-order framing error given that abstracts are what desk decisions turn on.
already_addressed: The intro is organized under four paragraph headings (Automation versus Augmentation; Optimizing Automation and Fragmentation; Non-Monotone Effects of AI Progress; Empirical Evidence), which is a partial substitute for a roadmap, and Table 1 usefully summarizes the two horizons. But headings over intro paragraphs do not tell the reader where Sections 3-8 go, and the paper never numbers its contributions.
fix: Four edits. (1) Add a "we show" paragraph on p.2, immediately after the two model-description paragraphs, numbering the contributions in the order they appear. (2) Add a roadmap paragraph at the end of the introduction. (3) Fold Section 2 into the introduction as a positioning paragraph plus footnotes, or move it after Section 3, which buys three body pages and gets the model onto p.7. (4) Rewrite the abstract's last sentence: replace the CES clause with the wage/welfare result once Finding 1 is addressed, or, if it is not, simply cut the clause. Also rewrite the conclusion to state the model's two binding limitations (fixed step set, no equilibrium wage determination) and what the framework would need to answer the job-breadth question Section 5.3 leaves open, and uncomment the JEL codes and keywords.

title: The headline fragmentation regression mixes two incompatible exposure definitions and the body never says which is which
location: 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.2, eq (5) and the notes to Table 3 (tab:fragmentation_index_regression_exposure); C_sample_construction.tex para 3
claim: Three variables in eq (5) use two different exposure definitions and the reader cannot tell from the text. The body says only that "ai_exposure_o is the share of AI-exposed tasks," undefined; the EFI paragraph then says "We count as AI-exposed both E1- and E2-exposed tasks, which together account for 44% of the tasks"; the control is described as "the number of AI-exposed (E1- or E2-labeled) steps." Only the notes to Table 3 reveal the regressor itself is different: "The variable 'AI Exposure' denotes the share of AI-exposed (E1) steps in the occupation, while... The empirical fragmentation index (Definition 1) measures fragmentation based on potential AI chains formed by E1- and E2-exposed tasks." Appendix C then states a blanket rule that contradicts two of the three: "Unless explicitly mentioned otherwise, in all analyses we treat tasks with a human-assigned E1 label as exposed to AI and those with E0 or E2 labels as unexposed to AI." So within one regression, E2 tasks are simultaneously unexposed (regressor) and exposed (EFI and the count control).
why_it_matters: beta_2 is the paper's Prediction #2 result. Its interpretation, "conditional on exposure, dispersion lowers execution," requires that the conditioning variable and the dispersion variable be built from the same exposure concept. As specified, EFI can move purely because an occupation's E2 share moves, which the E1-share regressor does not absorb, so beta_2 partly picks up an omitted exposure margin rather than arrangement. The num_ai_able_steps control, which the paper says "ensures beta_2 is identified from how the AI-able steps are arranged rather than from how many of them there are," is E1-or-E2 and therefore does not restore the conditioning either.
already_addressed: The footnote justifying E1+E2 for the EFI is there and is sensible ("restricting attention to E1-exposed tasks alone (14% of tasks) would leave potential AI chains too sparse"), and Appendix D.2 reports an execution-based EFI Definition 2 as a cross-check. But no specification uses a consistent exposure concept across all three variables, and the mismatch is never named as such.
fix: Report the regression with all three variables built on E1+E2, and again with all three on E1 only, side by side, and say in the body which combination Table 3 shows. If the E1-only version is too sparse to estimate the EFI, say so explicitly and report it anyway. Also reconcile the Appendix C blanket sentence with actual practice, since as written it misdescribes the paper's own headline table.
